## Big Question {.role-slide}

How can a regression respect the possible values and variation of a linguistic response?

## Surprising Fact {.role-slide}

A straight line can predict negative counts, probabilities greater than one, and differences between ordinal categories whose distances were never measured.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Changing the response family and changing the scale of the conditional mean solve different parts of the problem.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. Assemble a generalized linear model one component at a time.
2. Model binary, ordinal, and count responses.
3. Diagnose count variation beyond a Poisson model.
4. Model bounded responses that include endpoints.

## When ordinary linear regression fails {.section-slide}

Begin with the measurement

## Data {.role-slide}

A completion is *in* or *for*. A corpus outcome is a count. A judgment is *no*, *maybe*, or *yes*.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

[Ordinary linear regression](../../regression-models/simple-linear-regression.html) assigns a [normally distributed](../../random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.html) response around an unrestricted conditional mean. These measurements impose other supports and variance relations.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/why-generalized-linear-models.html)

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Choose a response family from the measurement process. Then connect its conditional mean to the linear predictor on a scale where the predictor may vary freely.

## Link functions {.section-slide}

Connecting two scales

## Question {.role-slide}

How can an unrestricted linear predictor describe a probability in $(0,1)$ or a positive expected count?

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**link function**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) maps the constrained conditional mean to the [linear-predictor scale](../../regression-models/design-matrices.html).

$$
g(\mu_i)=\eta_i
\qquad
\mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i)
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

The link sends a mean to the linear-predictor scale. The inverse link returns a prediction to the response scale. Which direction does software use for `type = "response"`?

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/link-functions.html)

## Components of a generalized linear model {.section-slide}

Family, linear predictor, and link

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**generalized linear model**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) combines a response distribution, the previously introduced [linear predictor](../../regression-models/design-matrices.html), and a link function.

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Choose the response family.
2. Write $\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta$.
3. Set $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$.
4. Interpret predictions after applying $g^{-1}$.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Naming only a link is incomplete. The family states response variation, while the link states how the mean is related to predictors.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/generalized-linear-models.html)

## The exponential family {.section-slide}

A common mathematical form

## Idea {.role-slide}

The [**exponential family**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) writes a density or mass function as

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=h(y,\phi)\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}\right\}.
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

The derivative $b'(\theta)$ gives the mean. The second derivative helps determine the variance. Thus each response family links its mean to a particular variance relation.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A [**canonical link**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) sets the linear predictor equal to the natural parameter. Canonical does not mean required for every analysis.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/exponential-family.html)

## Sufficient statistics {.section-slide}

What the likelihood retains

## Data {.role-slide}

For independent Bernoulli responses with one probability, the likelihood depends on the sequence only through the number of successes.

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**sufficient statistic**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/book/export/html/844) retains all likelihood information about a parameter under the assumed model.

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 415</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat415/book/export/html/844
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Sufficiency is model specific. It licenses a likelihood reduction, not deletion of the token-level data needed for other questions and checks.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/sufficient-statistics.html)

## Iteratively reweighted least squares {.section-slide}

Fitting a generalized linear model

## Idea {.role-slide}

[**Iteratively reweighted least squares**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) replaces the nonlinear likelihood problem with a sequence of local weighted least-squares problems.

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Implementation {.role-slide .compact}

1. Begin with provisional coefficients.
2. Compute fitted means, working responses, and weights.
3. Solve weighted least squares.
4. Repeat until the updates stabilize.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Algorithmic convergence means the updates stabilized. It does not establish that the model is identified, fits the responses, or answers the linguistic question.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.html)

## Deviance {.section-slide}

Comparing a fitted model with saturation

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Deviance**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) compares a fitted model with the saturated model through their maximized log likelihoods.

$$
D=2\{\ell_{\mathrm{sat}}-\ell_{\mathrm{fit}}\}
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

Residual deviance depends on sample size and response structure. Its isolated magnitude is not a model comparison or a universal goodness threshold.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Differences in deviance compare nested likelihoods when the response, observations, and regularity conditions are held fixed.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/deviance.html)

## From probabilities to log odds {.section-slide}

The scale of logistic regression

## Idea {.role-slide}

[**Odds**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) compare event and nonevent probabilities. Their logarithm is the [**logit**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214).

$$
\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}
\qquad
\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

A probability of $.75$ gives odds of $3$. A one-unit increase in log odds multiplies the odds by $e$. It does not add a constant probability.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Odds ratios are constant under an additive logit model. Probability differences depend on the starting probability.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/odds-and-log-odds.html)

## Logistic regression {.section-slide}

A Bernoulli response with a logit link

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Logistic regression**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) uses

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i.
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

$e^{\beta_1}$ is the odds ratio for a one-unit change in $x$. Apply the inverse logit to declared predictor values before discussing probability differences.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The event coding determines the coefficient signs. Reversing zero and one reverses log odds but leaves the fitted event probabilities recoverable.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/logistic-regression.html)

## Verb type and temporal preposition choice {.section-slide}

SuperTelicity cloze responses

## Data {.role-slide}

Participants completed event descriptions with temporal phrases. The binary analysis asks whether result and manner verbs differ in the probability of an *in* rather than *for* completion.

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

The observed and fitted *in* probabilities are $.704$ for result verbs and $.337$ for manner verbs. The fitted odds ratio is about $.214$.

<div class="source">SuperTelicity cloze data</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. ../../slides/lecture11/supertelicity/README.md
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The pattern is consistent with the culmination contrast. But row-level uncertainty is inadequate because participants and verbs repeat.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/logistic-regression-example.html)

## Two predictors in logistic regression {.section-slide}

Partial comparisons on the log odds scale

## Question {.role-slide}

Does subject status predict pronominalization when modeled recency is held fixed?

## Method {.role-slide}

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{subject}_i+\beta_2\text{recency}_i
$$

Each coefficient is a partial comparison at fixed values of the other modeled predictor.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Inspect joint predictor support. A coefficient may rely heavily on the additive functional form when the corpus contains few comparable predictor profiles.

<div class="source">Bresnan et al. 2007</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://web.stanford.edu/~bresnan/qs-submit.pdf
:::

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/logistic-regression-with-multiple-predictors.html)

## Deviance residuals {.section-slide}

Locating observation-level mismatch

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Deviance residuals**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) are signed observation-level contributions whose squares sum to model deviance.

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 12</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Plot residuals against fitted values and theory-bearing predictors. Inspect large contributions in the original linguistic observations.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Deviance residuals help locate model failure. Their usefulness does not depend on forming a perfectly normal histogram.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/deviance-residuals.html)

## Ordinal regression {.section-slide}

Ordered categories without invented distances

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Coding *no*, *maybe*, and *yes* as 1, 2, and 3 imposes equal spacing. Dropping *maybe* changes the response.

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Ordinal regression**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1) models cumulative category probabilities with ordered cutpoints.

<div class="source">Penn State STAT 504</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The [**proportional odds assumption**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1) uses one predictor coefficient at every cumulative boundary. Check whether that shared shift is plausible.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1
:::

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/ordinal-regression.html)

## Poisson regression {.section-slide}

Positive conditional means for counts

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Poisson regression**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) combines a Poisson response with a log link.

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_i),
\qquad
\log\lambda_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

$e^{\beta_1}$ is the expected count ratio for a one-unit predictor change. The observation window must be comparable before raw expected counts can be compared.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The Poisson family assumes that conditional variance equals conditional mean. That restriction must be checked after the mean relation is specified.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/poisson-regression.html)

## Exposure offsets {.section-slide}

Separating rate from opportunity

## Question {.role-slide}

How should token counts be compared when documents contain different numbers of words?

## Answer {.role-slide}

An [**exposure offset**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) adds log exposure with its coefficient fixed at one.

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log t_i+\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

An offset defines the opportunity relative to which a rate is modeled. It is not an ordinary predictor with an estimated coefficient.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/exposure-offsets.html)

## Poisson regression for linguistic diversity {.section-slide}

Languages, growing season, and geographic area

## Data {.role-slide}

Nettle’s data contain language counts for 74 countries. Mean growing season represents the ecological contrast, and geographic area supplies exposure.

<div class="source">Winter 2020, Sections 13.3 and 13.4</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf
2. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i
$$

The stored area uses base ten, so the natural-log offset is $\log(10)\operatorname{Area}_i$.

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

A one-month increase in mean growing season is associated with an expected language rate about $1.284$ times as large at equal geographic area.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/poisson-regression-example.html)

## Checking Poisson dispersion {.section-slide}

Conditional variance under the fitted mean

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**Pearson residual**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) scales the raw discrepancy by the Poisson standard deviation.

$$
r_i=\frac{y_i-\widehat\mu_i}{\sqrt{\widehat\mu_i}}
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

The [**Pearson estimate of dispersion**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) summarizes squared Pearson residuals relative to residual degrees of freedom.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A large dispersion estimate identifies a variance mismatch. Residual plots and grouping structure are needed to locate its source.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/count-overdispersion.html)

## Quasi Poisson variance {.section-slide}

Rescaling uncertainty without changing the mean

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**quasi-Poisson model**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) keeps $\mathbb{E}(Y_i)=\mu_i$ and sets $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi\mu_i$.

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

Coefficient estimates remain tied to the same log-linked mean. Standard errors change because the variance is multiplied by the estimated dispersion.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The quasi-Poisson specification does not define a complete response distribution. It cannot supply an ordinary likelihood for likelihood-based comparison.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/quasi-poisson.html)

## Zero-inflated counts {.section-slide}

Two routes to an observed zero

## Possibility {.role-slide}

A verb may be structurally unable to occur in a construction, or it may be eligible but absent in a finite corpus.

## Method {.role-slide}

A [**zero-inflated model**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) combines a structural-zero process with a count process that may also generate zero.

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The two routes are unobserved. Use this model only when the design or linguistic theory motivates both processes, then check both components.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/zero-inflated-counts.html)

## Negative binomial regression {.section-slide}

Variance that grows faster than the mean

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Negative binomial regression**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) may use

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\mu_i+\frac{\mu_i^2}{\kappa}.
$$

<div class="source">Winter, Chapter 13</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234
:::

## Data {.role-slide}

Storme’s French liaison analysis compares reconstructed lexical-frequency counts for liaison and nonliaison morphemes while controlling final consonant.

<div class="source">Storme 2024 and released Study 1 data</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11525-024-09429-8
2. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12733801
:::

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

The Poisson dispersion estimate is enormous. The negative binomial model permits that variation and estimates a conditional mean ratio of about $9.35$ for liaison morphemes.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/negative-binomial-regression.html)

## Bounded responses {.section-slide}

Support fixed by the measurement

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**bounded response**](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11050-025-09244-9) has possible values in a known interval $[L,U]$. Exact boundary values are outcomes when the instrument permits them.

<div class="source">Grove and White 2025</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11050-025-09244-9
:::

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A distribution with unbounded support assigns probability outside the instrument. A beta distribution has support $(0,1)$ and assigns no probability to exact endpoints.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Boundedness does not itself choose a likelihood. Interior values, endpoints, discreteness, censoring, and repeated units must be represented separately.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/bounded-responses.html)

## Why standard beta regression fails for sliders {.section-slide}

Endpoints are observations

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Standard beta regression assigns positive density only inside $(0,1)$. A slider that permits 0 and 1 produces values in $[0,1]$.

## Possibility {.role-slide}

Replacing 0 by $\delta$ and 1 by $1-\delta$ makes every endpoint likelihood contribution depend on an arbitrary constant.

<div class="source">Grove and White 2025, supplementary Section 1</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1007%2Fs11050-025-09244-9/MediaObjects/11050_2025_9244_MOESM1_ESM.pdf
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Moving endpoints changes the data and the likelihood. Standard beta regression is coherent only when the measurement process excludes exact endpoints.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/why-not-beta-sliders.html)

## Ordered-beta regression {.section-slide}

Endpoint mass and an interior beta distribution

## Method {.role-slide}

[**Ordered-beta regression**](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11050-025-09244-9) uses two ordered cutpoints for endpoint probabilities and a beta distribution for interior responses.

<div class="source">Grove and White 2025</div>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11050-025-09244-9
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

One location predictor shifts probability from the lower endpoint through the interior toward the upper endpoint. This common ordering is an assumption to check.

## Question {.role-slide}

Compare predicted mass at zero, predicted mass at one, and the predicted interior distribution. A good overall mean does not establish that all three are represented.

[Return to the notes](../../regression-models/ordered-beta-regression.html)

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

Responses that require more than a straight line

## Big Question {.role-slide}

How can a regression respect the possible values and variation of a linguistic response?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. Begin with the response’s possible values and variation.
2. Keep the response family separate from the link.
3. Interpret coefficients on their model scale and predictions on the response scale.
4. Diagnose the particular restriction before choosing a repair.
